analysis.one_liner: Bars the federal government from penalizing people and organizations that oppose same-sex marriage.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 37 of 54 Senate Republicans as cosponsors but never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would prohibit any federal action — including tax penalties, revoking a tax exemption, denying a grant, contract, loan, license, accreditation, or federal benefits — against any person or organization that believes, or acts in accordance with the belief, that marriage is the union of one man and one woman or that sexual relations should be reserved to such a marriage. 'Person' is defined to include for-profit corporations, not just churches or charities. Because it protects people who 'act in accordance' with those beliefs, it would let federally funded schools, charities, contractors, and businesses refuse to serve or employ people in same-sex marriages while keeping their tax exemptions, federal money, and licenses.
analysis.who_benefits: Religious schools, colleges, charities, adoption agencies, and businesses that object to same-sex marriage. They would keep tax-exempt status, federal grants and contracts, licenses, and accreditation even if they refuse to recognize or serve same-sex married couples, and they could sue the federal government for damages if it tried to penalize them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Religious objector schools, charities, and businesses

how_it_helps.text: Blocks the federal government from altering the tax treatment of, assessing any tax or penalty against, or revoking the tax exemption of any person who believes or acts in accordance with the belief that marriage is one man and one woman [S3].

Blocks the federal government from denying or terminating any federal grant, contract, subcontract, loan, license, certification, accreditation, employment, or benefit under a federal benefit program for such a person [S3].
Requires the government to treat any person as accredited, licensed, or certified for federal purposes even if the only reason they lost that status was their marriage-related belief or conduct [S3].

Gives objectors a right to sue the federal government directly in federal court for compensatory damages and other relief, without first exhausting administrative remedies, and to recover attorney's fees [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Same-sex married couples, who could be turned away or denied services, employment, or spousal benefits by schools, charities, contractors, and companies receiving federal funds, with the federal government barred from penalizing those organizations. Federal agencies would also lose their existing ability to enforce nondiscrimination conditions on grants and contracts.

drawbacks.text: Because the bill protects people who 'act in accordance' with their beliefs and defines 'person' to include for-profit corporations, federal grantees, contractors, and commercial businesses could refuse to serve or employ people in same-sex marriages while keeping federal money, licenses, and tax exemptions [S3].

The bill would tie the government's hands broadly: any 'federal benefit program' benefit must continue, and the government must keep treating objectors as licensed and accredited, regardless of what nondiscrimination rules those programs normally impose [S3].

Supporters' underlying concern was real: in 2015 the Solicitor General told the Supreme Court that whether a religious school could lose its tax-exempt status for opposing same-sex marriage was 'certainly going to be an issue,' and the bill's findings cite that statement [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill responded to a genuine fear among religious institutions that they could lose tax-exempt status or federal funding after the Supreme Court's 2015 same-sex marriage ruling, and a law narrowly protecting those institutions' tax status would have addressed it. But the bill went much further: it guaranteed every federal benefit, contract, license, and tax advantage to any entity — including for-profit corporations — that refuses to recognize or serve same-sex married couples, and it let them sue the government for damages over any attempted penalty. The breadth of the shield, and who pays for it, is the central cost an honest supporter had to acknowledge.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee in June 2015, but the committee never held a hearing or a vote on it, and it died when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Senator Mike Lee introduced the bill on June 17, 2015, nine days before the Supreme Court ruled in Obergefell v. Hodges that same-sex couples have a constitutional right to marry [S1][S3].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced, and no further action was ever taken on it [S5].
Thirty-seven of the Senate's 54 Republicans signed on as cosponsors, including Senators Cruz, Rubio, Graham, Hatch, and Sasse [S3][S4].
No Democrat cosponsored the bill, and it never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, religious-objector institutions did not get the federal carve-out they sought, and same-sex married couples' access to federally funded services, contracts, and programs remained governed by the ordinary rules rather than a blanket exemption. Supporters would add that religious institutions also faced no new federal penalty, since nothing changed in law before the bill died.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Objector institutions got no new federal shield

for.name: Sen. Mike Lee
for.role: U.S. Senator from Utah; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and framed it as protection for religious believers after the Solicitor General said tax-exempt status for objecting schools was 'certainly going to be an issue'

for.name: Donald Trump
for.what_they_did: Publicly pledged during the 2016 campaign to sign the First Amendment Defense Act into law if elected

against.name: Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill, leaving it pending in committee until the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: All 38 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans — 37 of the caucus's 54 members plus the sponsor — with no Democrat signing on, and the bill never reached a vote.

industries.note: The bill would have locked in their tax exemptions and federal grants even if they refused to recognize or serve same-sex married couples, with the IRS barred from touching their tax treatment [S3]. The gain comes at the expense of same-sex couples' access to those institutions.

Agencies could keep receiving federal grants and contracts while acting on the belief that marriage is one man and one woman — for example, restricting services to opposite-sex couples — without risking termination of funding [S3].

industries.industry: Federal contractors and for-profit businesses with religious objections
industries.note: 'Person' includes for-profit corporations, so commercial contractors could refuse spousal benefits or services to people in same-sex marriages and still keep federal contracts, licenses, and loans, and could sue for damages if penalized [S3].

industries.industry: Federal grant-making and civil-rights enforcement agencies
industries.note: Agencies would lose the ability to condition grants, contracts, loans, and licenses on nondiscrimination against people in same-sex marriages, and could face damages suits and attorney's-fee awards for attempting any such penalty [S3].
